title: Selective Generation for Controllable Language Models
research_question: Can selective generation for free-form language models obtain statistical control over semantically incorrect accepted answers by defining correctness through textual entailment and calibrating when the model should abstain?
methodology: The authors define an entailment-based false discovery rate, FDR-E, for a generator that either returns its answer or outputs an IDK-style abstention. SGen-Sup obtains a supervised risk bound, while SGen-Semi uses PAC conformal entailment-set learning and unlabeled examples to propagate pseudo-labels while bounding false entailment errors. Neuro-selection combines candidate confidence functions, including answer likelihood and self-consistency, to improve acceptance efficiency subject to a requested FDR-E constraint. Experiments use GPT-3.5-Turbo and Alpaca-7B on Natural Questions, with manually labeled textual-entailment datasets of 4,595 and 7,374 generated examples respectively, plus up to 10,000 or 27,000 unlabeled examples.

key_findings.finding: The paper provides a PAC-style theoretical guarantee that the learned selective generator's entailment-based false discovery rate is upper bounded with user-specified confidence under the stated assumptions.

In the reported experiments, SGen-Semi generally controlled the requested FDR-E while obtaining higher average selection efficiency than the compared certified and heuristic semi-supervised alternatives.

With only 75% of the labeled calibration examples used by fully supervised methods, SGen-Semi achieved selection efficiencies of 0.7334 for GPT-3.5-Turbo and 0.3173 for Alpaca-7B in the reported comparison.
Adding more unlabeled examples increased selective-generation efficiency in the reported experiments.
Textual entailment provides a more suitable semantic correctness criterion for free-form answers than exact match, which can reject semantically equivalent valid responses.
The neuro-selection mechanism improved average efficiency by choosing among multiple scoring functions rather than relying on a single fixed confidence measure.
The empirical FDR-E bound was not especially tight in all settings, particularly for Alpaca-7B, despite the formal guarantee.

limitations: The formal correctness guarantee assumes calibration and deployment examples are i.i.d.; the authors explicitly note that this assumption may fail in practical environments.
The guarantee therefore does not directly cover temporal drift or distributional change between calibration and deployment.
Producing gold entailment labels is expensive because generated and reference answers must be compared for logical entailment.
The semi-supervised procedure reduces but does not remove dependence on labeled entailment data.
Empirical FDR-E can be substantially below or otherwise loosely related to the requested bound, especially for Alpaca-7B, indicating conservatism or looseness in the bound.
The experiments cover one open-ended QA source dataset and two generators, limiting evidence for generalization to other long-form generation tasks.
Correctness is reduced to entailment with a reference answer, so completeness, citation support, evidence freshness, and omission of additional required facts are outside the metric.
The method does not explicitly address source-version changes or temporally evolving truths.
raw_claims: Selective generation returns an answer only when a learned selection rule accepts it and otherwise abstains.
FDR-E measures the rate of accepted generated answers that are not semantically entailed by the reference answer.
SGen-Sup and SGen-Semi provide statistically controlled selective-generation procedures.
SGen-Semi uses conformalized entailment sets to control pseudo-labeling errors when exploiting unlabeled data.
The experiments evaluate GPT-3.5-Turbo and Alpaca-7B generations derived from Natural Questions.
The authors manually construct entailment labels for generated and reference answer pairs.
Semi-supervised training uses fewer labeled examples than the fully supervised comparison.
Additional unlabeled examples improve selection efficiency in the reported experiments.
Exact match is inadequate for many semantically correct free-form answers.
The authors explicitly state that the i.i.d. assumption needed by the guarantee may be violated in practice.
Code and experimental datasets are released by the authors.
